nameStory: The small yellow pond-lily gets its name from its cheerful yellow flowers that bloom on the surface of quiet ponds and lakes. The 'small' part distinguishes it from its larger cousins in the yellow pond-lily family. Unlike true water lilies with their showy white or pink blooms, these hardy northern beauties stick to sunny yellow petals that peek above the water like little floating suns.
description: Small yellow pond-lily is an aquatic perennial that lives entirely in the water, growing from thick underwater stems called rhizomes. Its heart-shaped leaves float on the water's surface like green lily pads, while cup-shaped yellow flowers rise just above the water on sturdy stalks. This is one of New England's rarest water plants, making any sighting a special discovery. The whole plant creates a classic pond scene with floating leaves and bright yellow blooms dotting the water's surface.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small cup-shaped yellow flowers with thick, waxy petals that feel leathery to the touch. The blooms stick up just above the water surface on short, sturdy stalks and have a faint sweet fragrance.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Heart-shaped floating leaves that feel smooth and waxy on top, with a deep notch where the leaf stem attaches. The undersides often have a reddish tint and feel slightly fuzzy.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Grows entirely in water with leaves floating flat on the surface and flowers rising slightly above. Forms small colonies connected by thick underwater stems.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Develops small, bottle-shaped fruits that start green and ripen to brown, eventually splitting open to release seeds that float away.

habitat: Found in shallow, quiet waters of ponds, slow streams, and lake edges with soft, muddy bottoms. Prefers slightly acidic water in cooler northern regions of New England. Often grows alongside cattails, pickerelweed, and other wetland plants in areas with full sun to partial shade.

seasonality.spring: New leaves begin emerging from underwater rhizomes as water warms, unfurling at the surface in late spring.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming period with bright yellow flowers appearing from June through August, floating leaves fully developed.
seasonality.fall: Flowers fade and seed pods ripen, leaves may yellow slightly but often remain green well into fall.
seasonality.winter: All above-water parts die back, plant survives as dormant rhizomes buried in pond mud beneath the ice.

funFact: This little water lily is so rare in New England that it's been spotted fewer times than a snow leopard sighting - with only 5 confirmed observations across the entire region, making it one of our most elusive native plants!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with its larger cousin spatterdock, which has bigger leaves and flowers, or variegated yellow pond-lily. Look for the smaller size of everything - flowers, leaves, and overall plant - plus the more northern habitat preference to distinguish small yellow pond-lily.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called a 'lily,' yellow pond-lilies are not related to true lilies at all - they're in the water lily family. The extreme rarity of this species in New England makes proper identification crucial, as it's considered extirpated (locally extinct) in Connecticut and of special concern elsewhere.
compareHints: Small yellow pond-lily is much smaller in all parts compared to spatterdock, which has leaves up to a foot across and larger, more globe-shaped flowers. Variegated yellow pond-lily has leaves with wavy edges and often reddish markings, while small yellow pond-lily has smooth-edged, plain green leaves. The small species also prefers cooler, more northern waters than its relatives.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Variegated yellow pond-lily differs from spatterdock by having smaller flowers and more pronounced leaf mottling, while small yellow pond-lily has much tinier leaves (usually under 4 inches) and grows in shallower water.
Spatterdock is the giant of New England's yellow pond-lilies, with the largest leaves and most robust growth habit.
